classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate five small positive-integer powers directly.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 evaluates cubes of the five specified bases; this directly assesses evaluating index notation.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a positive-integer power as repeated multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate five small positive-integer powers directly.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive positive-integer powers of three.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 varies the exponent while retaining base three; evaluation is the assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Expand each power as repeated multiplication, as in the introductory sequence of powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive positive-integer powers of three.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of a negative base, retaining the parentheses and alternating signs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 evaluates powers rather than negative indices; the negative sign belongs to the base.
questions.methodNote: Apply the repeated-factor definition to the entire parenthesised negative base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of a negative base, retaining the parentheses and alternating signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine index laws with numerical coefficients, quotients and nested powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d and m use product or quotient laws; e, f and n use power-of-a-power; g–j distribute powers; k, l, o and p combine coefficient arithmetic and index laws. Algebraic products and quotients is the closest skill covering the complete question.
questions.methodNote: Apply Theorem 1: add indices in products, subtract in quotients, multiply in nested powers, and distribute a power over products or quotients. Evaluate numerical coefficients as in Examples 1 and 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine index laws with numerical coefficients, quotients and nested powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines coefficient simplification, powers of products and quotient laws.

questions.mappingNote: Each part is an algebraic quotient requiring positive-index simplification; part (h) uses the power-of-a-quotient law.
questions.methodNote: Apply the index laws in Theorem 1; expand powers of coefficients and products, then cancel common factors as in Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines coefficient simplification, powers of products and quotient laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines multiplication, reciprocal division and powers of multivariable fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a), (c)–(h), (j), (k) and (o) simplify products; (b), (i), (l)–(n) and (p) require reciprocal division. The classification covers the most advanced combined operations.
questions.methodNote: Expand powers, multiply fractions and cancel common factors. For division, multiply by the reciprocal, following Example 2(b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines multiplication, reciprocal division and powers of multivariable fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies index laws to symbolic exponents and nested powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(d) use product and quotient laws; (e)–(l) combine them with powers of powers. Symbolic exponents are directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Add indices when multiplying equal bases, subtract when dividing, and multiply indices for powers of powers, as in Theorem 1 and Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies index laws to symbolic exponents and nested powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires expressing composite bases as products before cancelling powers and evaluating.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) cancels equal bases; (b) rewrites 6 as 2 times 3; (c) rewrites 6 and 9; (d) uses the power-of-a-quotient law in reverse.
questions.methodNote: Use the product, quotient and power laws from Theorem 1 to simplify exact numerical powers before evaluating.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires expressing composite bases as products before cancelling powers and evaluating.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify repeating units-digit cycles and locate large powers within them.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 applies that numerical-power method to four bases; the closest catalogue skill is applying index laws with numerical bases.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 identifies a repeating units-digit cycle and uses the exponent's remainder to select its position.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify repeating units-digit cycles and locate large powers within them.

classification.difficultyReason: Disprove a general claim with a counterexample and construct examples satisfying it.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses numerical application and the distinction between multiplying exponents and exponentiating an exponent.
questions.methodNote: Theorem 1(c) and Example 1(c) multiply indices for a power of a power; numerical evaluation checks proposed equalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Disprove a general claim with a counterexample and construct examples satisfying it.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert nested powers to powers of ten and relate the exponent to the number of digits.

questions.mappingNote: Numerical index-law application is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill; digit counting supplies the interpretation.
questions.methodNote: Apply the power-of-a-power law from Theorem 1(c) and Example 1(c), then count the digits of the resulting power of ten.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert nested powers to powers of ten and relate the exponent to the number of digits.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied comparisons scaffold the bounds, but students must choose two decompositions of 55, propagate inequalities through powers and connect bounds between consecutive powers of ten to digit count.

questions.mappingNote: Numerical index-law application is the closest existing skill for constructing bounds and interpreting their digit count.
questions.methodNote: Use the multiplication and power-of-a-power laws from Theorem 1 and Example 1. Parts (a) and (b) supply the comparisons needed for the two bounds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two power comparisons to bound a large power between consecutive powers of ten.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must translate equal shares and their products into an equation with variable exponents, then recognise how cancelling a common power isolates x.

questions.mappingNote: The equal parts give repeated products represented by powers; cancelling and rearranging uses the algebraic index laws taught in this section.
questions.methodNote: Use the product, quotient and power-of-a-quotient laws established in Theorem 1 and applied in Examples 1 and 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate products of equal parts into powers and rearrange an equation with a variable exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct numerical application of zero powers and negative powers, including fractional reciprocals.

questions.mappingNote: Each numerical part directly evaluates zero or negative powers; the fractional-base parts use the reciprocal method demonstrated in Example 1.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 defines zero powers as 1 and negative powers as reciprocals. Example 1 evaluates integer powers and nested fractional reciprocals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct numerical application of zero powers and negative powers, including fractional reciprocals.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines integer index laws across products, quotients and powers, then converts negative indices to positive indices.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h apply product or quotient laws; i–l apply powers of powers and products; m–p combine these laws with reciprocals. The selected skill covers their negative algebraic indices.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 Examples 2 and 3 apply product, quotient and power laws, then write negative powers as reciprocals. Page 6 states the integer index laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines integer index laws across products, quotients and powers, then converts negative indices to positive indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines powers of products, multiplication and division with negative integer indices.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses compound algebraic simplification with integer index laws. Parts a–e emphasise powers and like-base combinations; f–g include numerical coefficients and products; h–l include algebraic quotients and reciprocals.
questions.methodNote: Use the zero and negative-power definitions, expand powers of products, add or subtract like-base indices, and replace division by a fraction with multiplication by its reciprocal. This follows Examples 1–4 and the integer index laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines powers of products, multiplication and division with negative integer indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines symbolic integer exponents using product, quotient and power laws.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly combines symbolic integer exponents. Question 4 does not require positive indices.
questions.methodNote: Use product, quotient and power-of-a-power laws with integer indices; apply the zero-index rule in part j.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines symbolic integer exponents using product, quotient and power laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplifies compound fractions using reciprocal powers and difference-of-squares factorisation.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts extend the reciprocal manipulations in Examples 1–3 to compound algebraic fractions; difference-of-squares factorisation enables cancellation.
questions.methodNote: Convert negative powers into reciprocals, simplify compound fractions and cancel common factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplifies compound fractions using reciprocal powers and difference-of-squares factorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary reciprocal-power terms and evaluate the central zero-power term.

questions.mappingNote: The finite sum directly assesses reciprocal-power simplification, with recognition of complementary pairs.
questions.methodNote: Use the negative-power reciprocal definition from page 4 and positive-index rewriting demonstrated on page 5; use the zero-power definition for the central term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary reciprocal-power terms and evaluate the central zero-power term.

classification.difficultyReason: An exhaustive answer requires unsignposted factorisation followed by coprimality and size arguments for positive indices, exclusion of zero and a separate parity argument for negative indices.

questions.mappingNote: Factorisation is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill. The teacher argument is completed by considering undefined and negative-index cases explicitly.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught index laws and reciprocal definition; follow the teacher solution's common-factor and difference-of-squares factorisation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor exponential expressions and exclude zero, positive and negative integer cases using divisibility.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate familiar roots using unit fractional indices.

questions.mappingNote: Every part evaluates a unit fractional power, including roots of fractions.
questions.methodNote: Use a^{1/n}=the nth root of a, as in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate familiar roots using unit fractional indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate fractional powers by taking a root and then raising to an integer power.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly apply a^{m/n}=(nth root of a)^m.
questions.methodNote: Take the denominator's root first, then raise to the numerator's power, following Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate fractional powers by taking a root and then raising to an integer power.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocal and root definitions to evaluate negative fractional powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use unit fractional powers; parts e–h also require an integer power after the root.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite a negative fractional power as a reciprocal, then evaluate its denominator using roots, following Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocal and root definitions to evaluate negative fractional powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert several radicals to fractional indices and combine powers, including quotients requiring positive-index answers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–j apply root conversion and product laws; k–l apply the quotient law, with k requiring a reciprocal to keep indices positive.
questions.methodNote: Convert radicals to fractional powers, add indices for products and subtract for quotients; rewrite a negative resulting index as a reciprocal. Follow Examples 3 and 8 and the index laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert several radicals to fractional indices and combine powers, including quotients requiring positive-index answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine fractional indices and express negative resulting indices as reciprocals.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses rational-index arithmetic; parts b, f, g, i and j require a positive-index reciprocal.
questions.methodNote: Apply product and quotient laws to rational indices, then replace negative powers by reciprocals, following Examples 3 and 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine fractional indices and express negative resulting indices as reciprocals.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert roots to fractional indices, multiply indices and evaluate exact powers.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts use the precise method demonstrated in Example 7.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 converts a root to exponent form, applies the power-of-a-power law and evaluates the resulting root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert roots to fractional indices, multiply indices and evaluate exact powers.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest parts link radical-to-index conversion, separate collection of each variable's exponents and conversion of negative results into positive-index denominators using the demonstrated method.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use one-variable rational-index laws; parts e–h directly extend Example 9's two-variable fractional simplification.
questions.methodNote: Examples 3, 8 and 9 convert radicals to rational powers, combine each variable's indices and convert negative indices to positive-index denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert compound radicals to rational indices and collect powers of two variables across products and quotients.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve equations with rational powers by raising both sides to a reciprocal power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c directly use Example 4; part d first uses the root-to-index definitions on pages 7–8.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 raises both sides to the reciprocal of the exponent on x, then applies the power-of-a-power law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve equations with rational powers by raising both sides to a reciprocal power.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert radicals to fractional indices and multiply by a complementary power to rationalise each denominator.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly apply fractional indices to rationalising denominators; this is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 on PDF page 9 converts the denominator to fractional-index form and multiplies numerator and denominator by the complementary power. Definitions and index laws support splitting roots of fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert radicals to fractional indices and multiply by a complementary power to rationalise each denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must factor the numerical radicands into the specified prime bases, convert roots into powers and collect each prime's exponent to identify a, b and c.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess fractional-index conversion and collection of numerical powers; fractional-indices is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the root-to-index definitions, Example 3's addition of exponents and Theorem 1's product and power laws to collect prime-base powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrite composite radicands using prime bases and combine several fractional exponents.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove exact bounds for a cube root by comparing cubes of positive rational numbers.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed concept is a fractional power and its exact bounds; fractional-indices is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: The definition of a cube root relates cubing to the exponent 1/3. Compare exact rational cubes, then take cube roots, as also shown in the matched teacher answer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove exact bounds for a cube root by comparing cubes of positive rational numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal conjugate bases and apply negative-power and product laws to an irrational exponent.

questions.mappingNote: Recognising and using reciprocal powers is the central assessed step; reciprocal-index-expressions is the closest catalogue match, although the printed exponent is irrational.
questions.methodNote: Use the negative-exponent definition and product law, with the reciprocal-conjugate observation supplied by the matched teacher answer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal conjugate bases and apply negative-power and product laws to an irrational exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves equivalence of root and power expressions using the supplied hint.

questions.mappingNote: Directly establishes the equivalence of the two definitions of fractional powers introduced on teaching page 8.
questions.methodNote: Use the nonnegative-root definition and integer power-of-a-power law, then take the nonnegative root as directed by the hint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves equivalence of root and power expressions using the supplied hint.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves a nested-root identity rather than assuming the rational power-of-a-power law.

questions.mappingNote: Establishes a fractional-index identity from the root definition without circularly assuming the identity being proved.
questions.methodNote: Convert reciprocal exponents to roots, apply integer powers to remove each root, then take the nonnegative mnth root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves a nested-root identity rather than assuming the rational power-of-a-power law.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a proof of the product rule for nonnegative nth roots.

questions.mappingNote: Proves the fractional-index product identity that supports the rational index laws presented on teaching page 10.
questions.methodNote: Use the integer power of a product and the definition of nonnegative nth roots, then take the nonnegative nth root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a proof of the product rule for nonnegative nth roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a proof that equivalent fractional representations give the same rational power.

questions.mappingNote: The root definition on pages 7–8 directly supports independence of the fractional representation.
questions.methodNote: Use non-negative roots and integer powers to establish the definition of a rational power without assuming the result being proved.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a proof that equivalent fractional representations give the same rational power.

classification.difficultyReason: Converting the infinite product into powers exposes a weighted infinite exponent sum; students must discover a shift-and-subtract summation strategy and then relate the second product to the square of the first.

questions.mappingNote: Printed question 19 maps to part a; printed question 20 maps to part b. Both assess rational-power simplification, with an enrichment extension to infinite products.
questions.methodNote: Convert roots to rational powers and combine powers of a common base. The answer evidence extends this to a convergent exponent sum and then squares the preceding product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires converting infinite radical products to powers and evaluating an infinite exponent sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct common-base equations with integer solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 1(a–i) directly assesses solving an exponential equation by this common-base method.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 rewrites both sides with a common base, equates exponents and solves the resulting linear equation; reciprocal powers use negative indices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct common-base equations with integer solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Related numerical bases and reciprocal powers produce rational or negative solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and h use base 2 directly; b, e and i use base 3; c, d, f and j use base 2; g uses base 5. All assess common-base exponential equations.
questions.methodNote: Use the power-of-a-power law to rewrite both sides with a common base, then equate exponents as in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Related numerical bases and reciprocal powers produce rational or negative solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Affine exponents and variables on both sides require a linear equation after conversion to a common base.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c, d, f, g and i use base 2; b, e and h use base 3. The directly assessed skill is solving exponential equations with affine exponents.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 1(b–c): expand products in exponents after conversion to a common base, equate exponents, then solve the linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Affine exponents and variables on both sides require a linear equation after conversion to a common base.

classification.difficultyReason: Repeated equal exponential terms must be combined before equating indices.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b reduce to base 2 and c to base 3. Combining equal terms is preparatory; solving the exponential equation is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Combine equal terms into a numerical multiple, apply index laws, and then use Example 1's common-base and equating-exponents method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Repeated equal exponential terms must be combined before equating indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert radicals to fractional powers and solve linear equations in the exponents.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 5(a–f) assesses the same common-base method with a square or cube root.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 rewrites radicals and numerical bases as powers of a common base, then equates exponents.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert radicals to fractional powers and solve linear equations in the exponents.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare consecutive integer powers to establish the least satisfying positive integer.

questions.mappingNote: All six inequalities require the same integer comparison method; the intended domain is made explicit.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 compares consecutive powers or reciprocals and identifies the first satisfying integer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare consecutive integer powers to establish the least satisfying positive integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an indicial inequality using complementary probability and establish the least number of independent trials.

questions.mappingNote: Replace the die's failure probability by one half and use the 99% threshold; a fair coin and independent tosses follow ordinary probability conventions.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 uses the complement of no successes and compares consecutive integer powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an indicial inequality using complementary probability and establish the least number of independent trials.

classification.difficultyReason: Use complementary probability to form an indicial inequality and compare consecutive powers of five sixths.

questions.mappingNote: This question changes the example's threshold to 90%; use a non-strict inequality to preserve 'at least'.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 uses one minus the probability of no sixes and compares consecutive integer powers of five sixths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use complementary probability to form an indicial inequality and compare consecutive powers of five sixths.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint supplies prime-factor representations, but students must derive non-negative integer exponent constraints, exhaust their possibilities using bounds and parity, and combine independent choices into all solutions.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is solving exponential equations, extended here to non-negative integer exponent constraints and exhaustive natural-number solutions.
questions.methodNote: Use the embedded prime-factorisation hint, combine powers and equate prime exponents. Pages 13–14 demonstrate common-base exponent comparison; the question supplies the additional unique-factorisation method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires prime factorisation, two independent integer exponent constraints and an exhaustive combination of their solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of positive decimals into scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h each directly assess decimal-to-scientific-notation conversion.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 expresses a decimal as a coefficient multiplied or divided by a power of ten, then writes m × 10^n with 1 ≤ m < 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of positive decimals into scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion from scientific notation into decimal form.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h each directly assess scientific-notation-to-decimal conversion.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 replaces the power of ten with multiplication or division by its decimal value, then evaluates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion from scientific notation into decimal form.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught significant-figure rounding procedure, identifying the first significant digit and handling a power-of-ten expression and trailing zeros.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess Example 6's rounding method. Scientific notation is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 expresses the number in scientific notation, then rounds its coefficient to the specified number of significant figures.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Round numerical values to specified significant figures using scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply powers of ten, normalise coefficients and convert decimal operands.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d apply page 17 Example 3(a); parts e–f first use page 16 Example 1's decimal conversion.
questions.methodNote: Multiply coefficients and add powers-of-ten exponents, then normalise to a coefficient between 1 and 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply powers of ten, normalise coefficients and convert decimal operands.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply with signed exponents, including exponent cancellation, and convert decimal operands.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d extend page 17 Example 3(a) to signed exponents; parts e–f also apply page 16 Example 1's conversion method.
questions.methodNote: Multiply coefficients, add signed exponents and normalise. Convert decimal operands to scientific notation first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply with signed exponents, including exponent cancellation, and convert decimal operands.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide coefficients, subtract positive and negative indices, and normalise results.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess scientific-notation division, including decimal operands.
questions.methodNote: Example 3(c–d): divide coefficients, subtract indices, then normalise; Examples 1–2 establish decimal conversion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide coefficients, subtract positive and negative indices, and normalise results.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine powers of products with multiplication or division and normalise.

questions.mappingNote: Each part combines the taught scientific-notation operations.
questions.methodNote: Example 3(a–c): apply product, quotient and power laws to coefficients and powers of ten, then normalise.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine powers of products with multiplication or division and normalise.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must express terms with matching powers of ten, add or subtract their coefficients and normalise the result, retaining a negative sign where required.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess scientific-notation arithmetic; addition and subtraction are not explicitly demonstrated on these teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Use the scientific-notation definition and decimal equivalences to match powers of ten, combine coefficients, and normalise. Retain a leading minus sign for negative results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match powers of ten before adding or subtracting, including negative results.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite radicands with square or cube coefficients and suitable powers of ten.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c directly follow Example 4; parts d–f extend its factor-and-root method to cube roots.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 rewrites the radicand as a perfect-square coefficient times an even power of ten, then takes roots separately. Apply the corresponding perfect-cube form to cube roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrite radicands with square or cube coefficients and suitable powers of ten.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply distance divided by speed to quantities in scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: The contextual calculation applies scientific-notation division after selecting time = distance/speed.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 divides coefficients and subtracts powers of ten, then normalises the result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply distance divided by speed to quantities in scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine percentage masses, kilogram-to-gram conversion and scientific-notation division.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) establishes the mass used in (b); part (c) repeats the same percentage, unit-conversion and molecule-count method.
questions.methodNote: Use decimal/scientific-notation conversion from Examples 1–2 and coefficient division with exponent subtraction from Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine percentage masses, kilogram-to-gram conversion and scientific-notation division.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine a consumption rate, annual distance and national car count.

questions.mappingNote: Calculate litres per car first, then multiply by the number of cars using scientific notation.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 multiplies coefficients and adds exponents, then expresses the result in scientific notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine a consumption rate, annual distance and national car count.

classification.difficultyReason: Following the taught digit-bound method, students choose exponent decompositions for upper and lower bounds and interpret the resulting powers of ten; part b explicitly directs them to sharpen the upper bound using 1024.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts use the digit-bound method. Part (b) needs a sharper upper bound than the direct supplied inequalities yield; the teaching example's exact value 1024 supplies it.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 decomposes a power into multiples of 10 and 13, bounds it using powers of ten, and infers its digit count. It explicitly evaluates 2^10 = 1024.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct upper and lower bounds using powers and infer decimal digit counts.
